Question: How do non-Kannadiga and non-Tamilian see the Kaveri issue? Whose side has more weightage of facts?
Answer: This is not a big problem. If both sides talk with an open mind, the problem can be solved. I have lived in both states. I have lived in Tamil Nadu for a year and almost 6 years in Bengaluru. Karnataka wants to renegotiate the Kaveri water sharing pact which was signed during British era. Karnataka says that the treaty during British time was done between a British Indian province and a princely state where British had favored Madras province (the land which it was ruling directly). Tamil Nadu doesn’t want to lose its share of water as they say that their farmers are dependent of the Kaveri water. I think we need to solve the issue from the point of being of an Indian. Karnataka residents and farmers are as Indian as Tamil farmers. Yes, Karnataka needs its fair share of water but at the same time we need to find alternate ways of water and ways to conserve water in agriculture. We need to use better ways of irrigation (like drip irrigation) at mass scale so that we can irrigate our fields with less water. Indian population is increasing and our cities needs more water and we need to develop our agriculture in such a way that it needs less water. We need to invest heavily in good variety of rice and better agriculture system. This can’t be done in a year and it will take decades with heavy investments. If Israel can turn Negev desert into agricultural hub then we can do wonders in India (particularly in green Eastern ghats of Tamil Nadu). This is not India-Pakistan issue but an internal matter. We need sensible political and social leadership in Chennai, Bengaluru and Delhi to solve the issue.

Question: Why is Sourav Ganguly considered an attacking batsman by his fans when he has a dismal strike rate of 73 in ODIs and 107 in T20s?
Answer: Let me talk about an ODI in 1999. It was 3rd ODI between India and New Zealand in Gwalior - Just look at the strike rate of all Indian batters. Sachin was struggling and made one run in 23 balls. If you take out Robin Singh (who came in 39th over), the highest strike rate of all other batters combined was 50. India was 142 for 5 in 38.3 overs. Indian team continued to struggle till around 45 overs. In the last 3 overs, India plundered around 75 runs and in the last three overs India made around 55 runs. In the end, Ganguly ended with 153 runs not out of 150 balls. I think Sachin scored 186 and Dravid scored 150 odd in the next match of the series. Even in 2023 (ODI or T20), if you score 75 runs in the last 5 overs we would consider it a very brutal hitting. Ganguly was doing that in the 1990s. Obviously the cricket has changed a lot in last 20 years. On those days, even scores of 250 were considered safe in ODI in many pitches. That 250 has become 330 now. Just look at the strike rate of fellow batters who batted in 1990s and 2000s in ODIs. Sachin’s strike rate is 80, Ponting 80, Jayasurya 91, Jayawardene 79, Kallis 73, Lara 78, Mohammad Yousuf 75, Inzamam 74. If you compare all these, then the Ganguly’s strike rate of 73 in ODI is not bad at all. And Ganguly was the opener and in many ODI innings he had to see off the pacers and he has played a lot of matches overseas. Let us look at another interesting stats in ODI. Ganguly has 190 sixes in 311 innings compared to 195 sixes in 452 innings of Sachin. Gaguly has more ODI sixes than Yuvaraj, Sehwag and even the great Kolhi may not touch 190s sixes in ODI. I have not seen a better batter hitting sixes to spinners (mainly left arm spinners) by charging a spinner. I have seen a lot of Sachin’s sixes of Shane Warne but Ganguly’s sizes over bowers head was always a delight. There was some scenario when opposition captain didn’t use their left arm spinner (I think it was Daniel Vettori and Fleming was the captain) for full ODI match. We the kids of 90s have seen so many immortal centuries of Ganguly like 124 against Pakistan in Dakha while chasing, 183 against Sri Lanka in Taunton in 1999 WC etc. Ganguly had 7 centuries in ODI in 2000. Till today, even Virat has not scored 7 centuries in a calender year. Sachin - Ganguly opening pair in ODI has been the best ODI partnership for India for all time. If you want to learn about cricket kindly don’t look at stats alone. You need to read about the impact the player created and the situation in which he performed. The stats hide much more than what it shows. I would rate Ganguly as one of the Indian batting greats.

Question: Should India Ban the Caste System by passing a Law, that Surnames should not reflect their Caste?
Answer: Let me give my personal example - I come from a small place in North Bihar. My family surname has been “Chaudhary” but my father decided to give me another surname “Gautam”. “Chaudhary” surname is itself a caste neutral surname. Chaudhary surname in Bihar is associated with many casts in Bihar like Bhumihars, Brahmins (General category), Kushwaha (OBC) and Dalits. In UP Jats have this surname and you will find this surname in Muslims in India and Pakistan. But my father decides to remove even this caste neutral surname and gave me a new surname “Gautam”. He was advised to do it by a Philosophy professor (who was a Brahmin). The idea was to use more caste neutral surname. By the way Gautam is our “Gotra” and after this many of my distant cousins have adopted this surname. My maternal grandfather has surname of “Singh” but all my maternal uncles (from the larger family) uses the surname “Sahi”. Surname change has been very common in Bihar. Lalu Yadav’s family surname was “Rai”. A good number of people in Bihar coming under “Yadav” caste umbrella use the title “Rai” (in my districts most of the Yadavs use this surname). Lalu Yadav changed his own surname so that his caste identity could be identified easily. Rai surname is also used by Bhumihars but Yadav surname is exclusively used by Yadav community. In Bihar, most of the girls and boys used Kumari and Kumar surname and later on they changed their surname (now it has become difficult to change the surname later in life due to birth certificate and Aadhar care. Even today you will find millions of Biharis with Kumar and Kumari surname. These surnames are the most caste neutral surname in India. India is a democratic country and we must give the Indians the choice to have any surname. A good number of surnames in India are caste neutral. Many surnames which we use today were not hereditary surnames but those were posts in history like Deshmukh, Chaudhary, Patil, Singh (to some extent) etc. Late these became hereditary surnames and these are used by many caste groups. In Bihar if someone’s surname is Singh then he/she can belong to these caste/religion - Rajput, Brahmin, Bhumihar, Jat Sikh and some OBC casts. The caste surname wold become less popular in case we eradicate caste from our normal day to day life. Let us all treat each other equally and eradicate caste based politics, reservations in next 50 to 70 years and then the caste based surname may become irrelevant
